list.listitem: Patients should be assessed for risk of thromboembolism and procedural/surgical bleeding with continuation or interruption of the antithrombotic agent according to their risk categories and medications, using shared decision making. C The indication for antithrombotic therapy assists in determining the former and risk scoring instruments can be used to determine bleeding risk along with lists that categorize procedures/surgeries according to bleeding risk. For specific procedures see the text.
Routine DOAC coagulation function testing, platelet function testing, or obtaining anti-factor Xa levels is not necessary prior to elective surgery/procedure to guide perioperative management. C

For most patients on aspirin (ASA) undergoing elective non-cardiac surgery, ASA can be continued. B In patients undergoing surgery with high-bleeding risk, ASA can be discontinued 7 or fewer days prior to surgery and resumed 24 hours afterwards. C

Interruption of clopidogrel is suggested for patients undergoing elective non-cardiac surgery 5 days prior to surgery. C Clopidogrel can be resumed 24 hours afterwards. Ticagrelor should be discontinued 3-5 days and prasugrel 7 days prior to planned surgery.

Temporary interruption of warfarin therapy prior to surgery is suggested for patients with low-moderate or high-risk of bleeding 5 days prior to surgery with rapid resumption (12-24 hours) of the usual dose of warfarin.C

Direct oral anticoagulants (DOAC) can be interrupted for one day prior to a procedure with low-moderate bleeding risk and 2 days for procedures with a high bleeding risk. C For individuals on dabigatran with poor renal function, 2- and 4-day interruptions pre-procedure are recommended, respectively. The DOAC can be resumed 24 or more hours after low-moderate-bleed-risk procedures, and 48-72 hours after high-bleed-risk procedures.C

For patients on warfarin interruption who are at high-thrombotic risk, bridging anticoagulation with full-dose, subcutaneous LMWH is suggested with the last dose given the morning of the day prior to the procedure (24 hours prior) at half the total daily dose. For those at high risk of bleeding, low-dose LMWH (e.g., enoxaparin, 40 mg daily or dalteparin 5,000 IU daily) can be used for venous thromboembolic (VTE) prophylaxis for the first 24-72 hours post-procedure, with full dose LMWH resumed 2-3 days post-procedure. C Resume LMWH bridging at 24 or more hours post-procedure/surgery and wait at least 48 to 72 hours before resuming LMWH bridging in patients who had a high-bleed-risk procedure/surgery.

ACCP 2022 guidelines suggest against perioperative heparin bridging for patients who require DOAC interruption, unless at high risk for VTE; for these patients, enoxaparin 40 mg daily or dalteparin 5,000 IU daily can be given for the first 48-72 hours post-procedure.C
During minor dental or surgical procedures, ACCP suggests continuing ASA, P2Y12 inhibitors, or VKAs. B Administration of an oral pro-hemostatic agent can be helpful prior to dental procedures. C
Consider aspirin + clopidogrel + oral anticoagulant postoperatively for patients on anticoagulation prior to stent placement who are at low risk of bleeding. B

Patients undergoing urgent surgery should receive vitamin K, fresh frozen plasma, or another prothrombin product if taking VKA. Patients taking antiplatelet medication should receive transfused platelets. C

Primary care clinicians are often asked to provide preoperative clearance (or, more appropriately, risk assessment) for their patients prior to planned surgical interventions. Temporary interruption of anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy during surgical procedures can expose patients to thrombotic risk. Thrombotic events can be devastating—an embolic stroke results in major disability or death in 70% of patients; thrombosis of a mechanical heart valve is fatal in 15% of patients; and perioperative myocardial ischemia is associated with a 2- to 4-fold increased risk for death. Continuation of these agents, however, is associated with increased bleeding risk.

Many patients are taking antiplatelet therapy for primary and secondary prevention of coronary artery disease, ischemic stroke, or symptomatic peripheral artery disease (PAD). Also common are patients taking long-term anticoagulation medication for atrial fibrillation, thromboembolism, and artificial heart valves. Risks to patients differ based on the reason for antiplatelet therapy; for example, interruption of antiplatelet drugs in patients with coronary stents significantly increases the risk for intracoronary stent thrombosis and myocardial infarction (MI). Conversely, patients with atrial fibrillation who are at low risk of stroke (i.e., CHA2DS2-VASc score, 0 for men; 1 for women) do not require antithrombotic therapy.

The American College of Chest Physicians (ACCP) updated their 2012 consensus recommendations in 2022 and addressed several new situations including perioperative management of patients who are receiving a DOAC and those who are receiving a P2Y12 inhibitor antiplatelet agent; they also provide guidance on perioperative laboratory testing. This chapter follows a similar format by presenting management recommendations for four broad categories: (1) a vitamin K antagonist (VKA), mainly warfarin; (2) if receiving a VKA, use of perioperative heparin bridging; (3) a DOAC; and (4) an antiplatelet drug, followed by additional information on specific procedures. The new ACCP recommendations do not cover patients who require urgent/emergency surgery or procedures.
The American College of Obstetrician and Gynecologists (ACOG) recommend that women on chronic antithrombotic therapy be seen at least 7 days before a planned gynecologic procedure to discuss options.

Authors comparing 3 clinical practice guidelines for perioperative antithrombotic therapy in urologic practice noted inconsistent recommendations on indications for antithrombotic medication, the preferred antiplatelet/anticoagulant agent and the type of urological procedure, creating uncertainty around best practice.
Patient preferences should be considered, especially when recommendations are not strongly supported by evidence.

Ideally, patients should be stratified according to their risk categories and medications. To allow for optimal risk stratification, , , and show perioperative management strategies for patients according to their heart disease and surgical risks. The perioperative period is generally considered from 1 week before until 4 weeks after a surgery or procedure.

Patients can be risk stratified empirically into high-risk and low-risk groups based on their indication for antithrombotic therapy, specifically their indication for VKA therapy. ACCP 2022 guidelines include tables that provide additional guidance for patient-specific periprocedural risk of thromboembolism and for risk-stratification of procedural/surgical bleeding.

Risk groups for thrombosis: There are no risk classification schemes that encompass the spectrum of benefit from antiplatelet agents. However, patients at high risk for cardiovascular events include those who have had a recent (within 3-6 months) placement of a coronary stent or who have suffered an MI or cerebrovascular accident within the past 3 months. Interruption of antiplatelet drugs in patients with coronary stents significantly increases the risk for intracoronary stent thrombosis and MI.

Other patients at high thromboembolic risk include those with atrial fibrillation, a CHA2DS2-VASc Score >6 or or CHADS2 score of 5 or 6, recent (within 3 month) history of DVT, mechanical mitral valve prosthesis, mechanical aortic valve prosthesis with an additional risk factor (reduced ejection fraction, atrial fibrillation, prior thromboembolic event), or caged ball or tilting-disc cardiac valves.

For patients with AF, the 2018 American College of Chest Physicians (ACCP) guidelines recommend use of CHA2DS2-VASc to identify patients at low risk of stroke who should not be offered antithrombotic therapy (i.e., men with a score of 0 and women with a score of 1).

Authors of a review of guidelines for management of antithrombotic therapy during elective total hip and knee arthroplasty agreed with the overall strategy of classifying surgical bleeding risk (joint arthroplasty is considered high risk as above), patient bleeding risk, patient thromboembolism risk, and considering surgical timing before deciding on an antithrombotic agent management plan. Surgical timing can be urgent (within 24 hours), semi-urgent (within 24 to 72 hours), or elective. Patient bleeding risk, as noted below, is determined using HAS-BLED with consideration of additional risk factors such as prior bleeding event within 3 months, platelet abnormality, supratherapeutic INR, prior bleeding from bridging therapy or prior bleeding from a similar procedure. In addition to use of the CHA2DS2-VASc Score of 1-4, no history of stroke or TIA, a prior venous thromboembolus more than 12 months prior and having a bileaflet aortic valve without atrial fibrillation or other stroke risk factors are used to determine low thromboembolism risk.

Risk scoring instruments can be used to determine bleeding risk. In a study comparing use of two bleeding risk scoring instruments—the Hypertension, Abnormal Renal/Liver Function, Stroke, Bleeding History or Predisposition, Labile INR, Elderly, Drugs/Alcohol Concomitantly (HAS-BLED) and the Outpatient Bleeding Risk Index (OBRI)—both performed reasonably well in predicting bleeding risk in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction who were in sinus rhythm and on treatment with warfarin or aspirin.

The ACCP 2018 guidelines suggest attention to modifiable bleeding risk factors and use of the HAS-Bled score to assess bleeding risk in patients with atrial fibrillation presenting with an acute coronary syndrome who may be candidates for percutaneous coronary intervention or stenting (see below).

listitem.strong: Similarly, surgical and other invasive procedures can be stratified into high and low risk based on their predicted associated intraoperative and postoperative bleeding risk.
Procedures with a high bleeding risk

list.listitem: Procedures with a high bleeding risk include coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) or heart valve replacement surgery; intracranial or spinal surgery; aortic aneurysm repair, peripheral artery bypass, and other major vascular surgery; major orthopedic surgery, such as hip or knee replacement; reconstructive plastic surgery; major cancer surgery (especially solid tumor resection); and prostate or bladder surgery.

The ACCP 2022 guidelines define high-bleed risk procedure/surgery as > or = to 2% and, in addition to the above, include as high risk the following: major surgery with extensive tissue injury, urologic or gastrointestinal surgery (especial anastomosis surgery), nephrectomy or kidney biopsy, bowel resection, percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy placement, endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, surgery in highly vascular organs (kidney, liver, spleen), any major surgery of >45 minutes duration, neuraxial anesthesia and epidural injections.

Authors of a systematic review of 19 articles evaluating the risk for bleeding in cardiac surgery related to dual antiplatelet therapy or DOACs found bleeding rates ranging between 18% and 41%. In the 10 papers evaluating antithrombotic drug reversal or removal in the setting of cardiovascular surgery, antithrombotic removal by intraoperative hemoadsorption was associated with a significant decrease in re-thoracotomy rate, overall procedure duration, administered transfusion volumes, chest-tube drainage, and length of hospitalization.

For management of antithrombotic therapy during elective total hip and knee arthroplasty, authors of the above guideline review recommended reversal of anticoagulation prior to surgery for urgent and semi-urgent total joint arthroplasty procedures.

Among 885 patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty, the 218 patients who discontinued antithrombotic drugs before surgery did not have a higher incidence of postoperative 30-day complications compared to those not on antithrombotic therapy.

In a case series of 158 patients undergoing pancreatic surgery, the 34 patients on perioperative antithrombotic treatment with either bridging therapy with unfractionated heparin or continued aspirin had a significantly higher post-pancreatectomy hemorrhage rate (29.4% vs. 6.5%) and mortality rate (11.8% vs. 2.4%) than patients not receiving thromboprophylaxis; perioperative antithrombotic treatment was an independent risk factor for post-procedural hemorrhage.

In a case series of 195 patients undergoing surgery for abdominal malignancy who had interruption of preoperative antithrombotic agents, there were no differences in blood transfusions or thromboembolic events between those receiving perioperative heparin bridging anticoagulation and no bridging therapy.
For patients undergoing lower-risk surgeries, continuing antithrombotic therapy may be reasonable, although study data are limited:

In a Japanese study of 1136 patients with saphenous varicose veins undergoing endovenous laser ablation, patients on antiplatelet (12.4%) and anticoagulant (8.4%) therapy had similar outcomes to those without antithrombotic therapy with few postoperative complications in either group (1.2% total).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs concluded that among patients undergoing atrial fibrillation ablation, uninterrupted novel oral anticoagulants (NOACs) are as effective as uninterrupted VKA treatment with respect to incidence of stroke or TIA, silent cerebral thromboembolic events, or minor bleeding.

Among patients who are taking aspirin for primary prevention, the rates of acute coronary syndrome leading to MI or death are twice as high in those who have stopped aspirin for greater than 12 days than in those who have continued treatment.
If aspirin is used for secondary prevention of CAD, the cardiac complication of aspirin withdrawal is 3 times higher in the general population and 90 times higher in patients with coronary stents.

Premature withdrawal of clopidogrel (<12 months for drug-eluting stents or <6 weeks for bare metal stents) is the most significant independent predictor of stent thrombosis, with a hazard ratio of 57.13 and mortality rate due to stent thrombosis of 45%.
Stopping clopidogrel to allow for major surgery during the first 3 weeks after percutaneous intervention (PCI) and stenting conferred a 30% to 86% mortality rate.
There is insufficient evidence to determine thromboembolic risks of discontinuing anticoagulants. Risk is likely higher if warfarin is discontinued for 7 or more days.

In a Finnish hospital database study of patients with atrial fibrillation who suffered an ischemic stroke or intracranial bleed, 6.0% of ischemic strokes and 2.9% of intracranial bleeds were preceded by an invasive procedure. Most (69%) of patients were on oral anticoagulants (OACs). Of the procedures leading to stroke, 42.3% were low-bleeding-risk procedures and OAC was interrupted in 84.7% of them; median time from procedure to stroke was 4 days. Heparin bridging was used in over half (54.5%) of OAC interruptions preceding intracranial bleeding while combination anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy was used by 43.5% of patients with postoperative intracranial bleeding.

ACCP 2022 guidelines suggest against routine use of DOAC coagulation function testing or platelet function testing prior to elective surgery/procedure to guide perioperative management (very low-certainty evidence). They also suggest against routine measurement of anti-factor Xa levels to guide perioperative low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) management in those who require bridging therapy.

Patients who take warfarin and have no history of a cardiac event or equivalent risk factors can be considered candidates for either continuing warfarin, if at minimal-bleeding risk, or stopping warfarin, if at low-moderate or high-risk of bleeding, at 5 days or more prior to any invasive procedure. Warfarin is restarted following appropriate hemostasis at the usual dose on the evening of or day after the procedure (low-certainty evidence). As always, this should be at the discretion of the surgeon, with knowledge of the inherent risks associated with the specific procedure.
The ACP 2022 guidelines note that interruption timing for non-warfarin VKAs differ, with a shorter period needed for acenocoumarol (2-3 days) and longer for phenprocoumon (10-12 days).
The 2016 Canadian Cardiovascular Society (CCS) guidelines agree with interruption of anticoagulation for procedures with an intermediate or high risk of major bleeding.

Patients who take VKAs for secondary prevention after a previous cardiac event or equivalent history should be managed individually with attention to the recommendations for using bridging therapy in .

ACCP notes that for patients who are elderly with co-morbidities, patients with very low-dose warfarin requirements, and those with a higher target international normalized ratio (INR) range, a longer period of warfarin interruption may be needed.

For patients requiring VKA interruption for an elective surgery/procedure who have an elevated INR of >1.5 1 to 2 days before the surgery/procedure, ACCP suggests against routine use of pre-operative vitamin K (very low-certainty evidence).
For specific procedures or surgeries, see individual categories below.

For ICD or pacemaker implantation, ACCP makes a strong recommendation based on moderate certainty of evidence to continue VKA therapy, assuming that the the patient’s INR at the time of the procedure is <3.0.

An American Academy of Neurology 2013 guideline suggests that patients on warfarin following stroke should probably continue the drug for dermatologic procedures, B and can possibly continue warfarin for EMG, prostate procedures, inguinal herniorrhaphy, and endothermal ablation of the great saphenous vein. C Continuing warfarin during colonoscopic polypectomy might increase bleeding risk. C ACCP 2022 guidelines recommend no bridging therapy during VKA interruption for these patients.
VKA bridging anticoagulation (bridging options provided in ACCP 2022 guidelines)

ACCP 2018 guidelines suggest that preoperative bridging is unnecessary in patients with AF treated with warfarin who do not have a particularly high risk of thromboembolism and who do not have a mechanical valve.

ACCP 2022 guidelines suggest full-dose, subcutaneous LMWH (e.g., enoxaparin, 1 mg/kg bid or 1.5 mg/kg daily or dalteparin, 100 IU/kg bid or 200 IU/kg daily) for those at high-thrombotic risk, with the last dose given the morning of the day prior to the procedure (24 hours prior) at half the total daily dose. For those at high risk of bleeding, low-dose LMWH (e.g., enoxaparin, 40 mg daily or dalteparin 5,000 IU daily) can be used for venous thromboembolic (VTE) prophylaxis for the first 24-72 hours post-procedure, with full dose LMWH resumed 2-3 days post-procedure. Resume LMWH bridging at 24 or more hours post-procedure/surgery and wait at least 48 to 72 hours before resuming LMWH bridging in patients who had a high-bleed-risk procedure/surgery (very-low certainty).

For patients on therapeutic-dose intravenous (IV) unfractionated heparin, ACCP suggests discontinuing heparin 4 or more hours before the procedure and resuming treatment at 24 or more hours afterwards.

For patients with a mechanical heart valve (very low certainty), atrial fibrillation (moderate certainty) or venous thromboembolus (very low certainty) who require VKA interruption, ACCP 2022 guidelines recommend against heparin bridging. However, in selected patients at high risk for thromboembolism such as those with a recent [< 3 month] history of stroke or transient ischemic attack, prior perioperative stroke, or CHA2DS2- VASc score of 7 or greater or CHADS2 score of 5 or 6), pre- and post-operative heparin bridging is suggested (see guideline for other exceptions).

The CCS Guidelines for atrial fibrillation suggest bridging therapy be instituted only when the INR is below therapeutic level AND the patient is at high risk of thromboembolic events (CHADS2 score of 4 or higher, mechanical heart valve, stroke/transient ischemic attack within 3 months, rheumatic heart disease) (low-quality evidence).

In a single-center pilot study including 45 patients undergoing a hybrid coronary artery stenting plus off-pump CABG surgery, 27 of whom received standard dual antiplatelet therapy postsurgery and 18 received tirofiban bridging plus dual antiplatelet therapy, there was a trend towards a lower rate of composite end points of stroke, postoperative myocardial infarction, and death within the tirofiban group (0% vs. 11.1%). Two patients in the standard group experienced a stroke.

DOACs are now recommended for most patients with newly diagnosed atrial fibrillation, based on the 2018 ACCP guidelines, and extended-phase low-dose anticoagulation with apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily or rivaroxaban 10 mg once daily is now recommended for all patients with unprovoked VTE. These agents require fewer days of discontinuation for surgery and a longer delay for re-initiation than warfarin.

With the exception of dabigatran in those with low creatinine clearance (<50 ml/min), ACCP 2022 guidelines recommend interruption of a DOAC for one day prior to a procedure with low-moderate bleeding risk and 2 days for procedures with a high bleeding risk. For individuals on dabigatran with poor renal function, they recommend 2- and 4-day interruptions pre-procedure, respectively
DOAC can be resumed 24 or more hours after low-moderate-bleed-risk procedures, and 48-72 hours after high-bleed-risk procedures.

ACCP 2022 guidelines suggest against perioperative heparin bridging for patients who require DOAC interruption (very low-certainty evidence). If bridging is needed for patients at high risk for VTE, enoxaparin 40 mg daily or dalteparin 5,000 IU daily can be given for the first 48-72 hours post-procedure.

Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors should be discontinued for at >24 hours if surgical bleeding risk is low to moderate and 48 hours preoperatively if bleeding risk is high; in patients with renal impairment, 72 to 120 hours is recommended.

With respect to intravenous therapies, eptifibatide and tirofiban should be discontinued 8 hours before surgery but abciximab requires discontinuation of 48 hours. The ACCP 2022 guidelines note that observational studies investigating bridging therapy found no clear benefit of short-acting IV glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors (tirofiban, eptifibatide) or cangrelor compared to IV unfractionated heparin or subcutaneous LMWH.

The CCS guidelines recommend no bridging for patients with nonvalvular AF receiving non-vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants who undergo elective surgery or invasive procedures requiring interruption of anticoagulation (moderate-quality evidence).

listitem.strong: Antiplatelet therapy (aspirin [ASA] and P2Y12 agents – clopidogrel, ticagrelor, prasugrel)

list.listitem: Patients NOT at high risk for cardiac events who are taking aspirin or clopidogrel can interrupt use of medications 5 days and 7 days, respectively, prior to surgery and resume aspirin and/or clopidogrel 24 hours afterwards. Ticagrelor should be discontinued 3-5 days and prasugrel 7 days prior to planned surgery.

Patients at high risk for cardiac events can continue aspirin up to and beyond the time of surgery (moderate-certainty evidence). ACCP 2022 guidelines recommend interruption of clopidogrel at least 5 days—and preferably 10 days—prior to surgery (very-low certainty evidence). In patients who require ASA interruption, stop aspirin 7 or fewer days prior to surgery (very low-certainty evidence).
For patients who require antiplatelet drug interruption, ACCP suggests resuming antiplatelet drugs within 24 hours post-procedure/surgery (very low-certainty evidence).

Patients scheduled for CABG can continue aspirin up to and beyond the time of surgery and restart 6 to 48 hours after surgery (low-certainty evidence). A large, well designed randomized trial published after the ACCP 2012 guidelines compared aspirin with placebo in 2100 patients undergoing CABG, and found no difference in cardiovascular or bleeding events. For patients receiving a P2Y12 inhibitor drug, ACCP 2012 suggested continuing aspirin for those on dual antiplatelet treatment with interruption of the P2Y12 inhibitor over continuation perioperatively.

Patients scheduled for PCI can continue aspirin up to and beyond the time of surgery (Grade 2C). If clopidogrel is interrupted prior to PCI, recommend resuming with a loading dose of 300 to 600 mg 24 hours after procedure (Grade 2C).

For patients with AF requiring oral anticoagulants where bleeding risk is low (HAS-BLED 0 to 2), ACCP 2018 guidelines suggest use of triple therapy for 1-3 months, followed by dual therapy with oral anticoagulant plus single antiplatelet (preferably clopidogrel) until 12 months, following which oral anticoagulant monotherapy (weak recommendation). When bleeding risk is high, ACCP suggests use of an oral anticoagulant plus single antiplatelet (preferably clopidogrel) for 6 months, following which oral anticoagulant monotherapy (weak recommendation). Additional recommendations based on bleeding risk can be viewed in the referenced document for patients with atrial fibrillation and acute coronary syndrome.

Patients with stents: ACCP 2022 guidelines suggest that for elective surgery/procedures in patients receiving ASA and a P2Y12 inhibitor for coronary stents placed within the last 6 to 12 weeks, either continue both antiplatelet agents or stop one antiplatelet agent within 7 to 10 days of surgery (very low-certainty evidence). For those with more remote stent placement (within the last 3 to 12 months), ACCP suggests stopping the P2Y12 inhibitor prior to elective surgery over continuation of the P2Y12 inhibitor. They suggest against routine bridging therapy. When possible, delay elective surgery for patients with coronary stents who require continued dual antiplatelet therapy.

In a meta-analysis (no RCTs) of patients on preoperative anticoagulation who had stent placement, the use of “triple therapy” (aspirin + clopidogrel + oral anticoagulant) vs. dual therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel only) resulted in fewer cardiovascular events (odds ratio [OR], 0.60; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.42-0.86) and lower all-cause mortality (OR 0.59; 0.39-0.90) but higher risk of major bleeding (OR 2.1; 1.05-4.29).
In all patients with coronary stents who have an interruption of antiplatelet therapy before surgery, recommend against routine bridging therapy.
For patients who have a pacemaker or internal cardiac defibrillator implantation, ACCP 2022 guidelines recommend continuation of VKA therapy.

AACP 2018 guidelines on antithrombotic therapy for atrial fibrillation recommend performing the procedure on uninterrupted VKA (within the INR therapeutic range), dabigatran or rivaroxaban (weak recommendation).

In a retrospective study of 1093 Chinese patients undergoing cardiac rhythm device implantation, the incidence of pocket hematoma was low and similar for patients taking aspirin (3.9%) or clopidogrel (1.2%) alone and those taking no anticoagulant. The incidence of pocket hematoma was higher for patients on dual antiplatelet therapy (16.2%) and the heparin bridging therapy (14.0%) and for those with thrombocytopenia.

In a case series of 723 consecutive adult patients on antithrombotic treatment who underwent implantation or surgical revision of a cardiac implantable electronic device (CIED), most patients (67.6%) were continued on antithrombotic treatment. Patients taking non-vitamin K oral anticoagulants only (88.7% had treatment interrupted with 25.6% receiving heparin bridging) had lower rates of minor pocket hematoma and hemorrhagic complications. Few patients had severe pocket hematomas and no patients had intracranial hemorrhage or thrombotic events.

In a network meta-analysis of 31 observational studies of antithrombotic therapy during CIED placement, aspirin had the lowest bleeding risk followed by warfarin, clopidogrel and novel oral anticoagulants (NOACs). Aspirin (4.26 [2.88-7.22]), warfarin (3.37 [2.17-5.23]), and clopidogrel (3.30 [1.49-5.88]) reduced bleeding risk compared to heparin bridging which had similar risk to continued NOACs. Continued warfarin (3.74 [1.96-7.16]), interrupted warfarin (4.89 [2.20-10.88]), and interrupted NOACs (12.5 [1.25-100]) reduced bleeding risk compared to heparin bridging.

In a retrospective study of 135 consecutive patients on antithrombotic treatment undergoing CIED implantation, use of topical tranexamic acid (52 patients) reduced rates of pocket hematoma (7.7% vs. 26.5%) and major bleeding complications (5.8% vs. 20.5%) compared to patients not receiving this application. There were no thromboembolic complications.

listitem.strong: Case series comparing patients undergoing various procedures who continued antithrombotic therapy compared to either bridging therapy or temporary cessation

list.listitem: Authors of a review of the urologic literature concluded that despite limited evidence, aspirin should be continued in patients with intermediate to high risk of coronary thrombosis during endoscopic procedures for the treatment of benign prostate enlargement (transurethral resection of the prostate, Thulium, Holmium and greenlight laser prostatectomy), bladder cancer (transurethral resection of the bladder), upper urinary tract urothelial cancer, and nephrolithiasis. In these patients, bridging with LMWH potentially led to more bleeding than continuation of the anticoagulant(s) and antiplatelet therapy.

Similarly, in a case series of 360 patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery whose chronic antithrombotic therapy was interrupted from 5 [2, 7] days before the surgery to 4 [2, 7] days postoperatively, the 113 (31.4%) who received perioperative bridging therapy with heparin had significantly increased risk of bleeding events (5.3% vs. 0.8%) which occurred in 8 patients total. Thrombotic events occurred in 2 patients (0.6%) who did not receive bridging therapy.

In patients undergoing dermatologic procedures in one case series, bleeding occurred in 7.14% although severe bleeding was rare (0.91% of 9154 surgeries). Bleeding was associated with current treatment with anticoagulation therapy, but the highest bleeding risk was among those who underwent LMWH bridging therapy (9.26%).

listitem.strong: Case series comparing patients on antithrombotic therapy with no antithrombotic therapy

list.listitem: In a case series of patients undergoing gastric endoscopic submucosal dissection, the incidence of delayed bleeding was significantly higher in patients on chronic antithrombotic therapy (9.5% [35/367] vs. 4.2% [30/722] not on antithrombotics. The incidence of bleeding was higher regardless of whether patients continued antithrombotic therapy, had heparin bridging or were withdrawn from antithrombotic therapy (9.2% (5/54), 10.8% (4/37), and 9.4% (26/276); thrombotic events only occurred in 1.6% of those who discontinued antithrombotic therapy.

In a case series of 1152 procedures, including hemorrhoid excision and ligation, at a single institution, post-operative bleeding events were more common in patients on antithrombotic therapy (5.92% vs. 2.66% of patients not on anti-thrombotic therapy; OR 2.3, 95% CI 1.21 to 4.38). However, there was no difference in bleeding events that required hospital admission or a repeat procedure, which occurred in 7 of 40 cases (17.5%).

In a case series of 55 patients undergoing endoscopic contact laser vaporization of the prostate, 21 of whom were on antithrombotic therapy, there were no significant differences in the occurrence of catheter obstruction due to blood clots or serious hematuria following catheter removal or in perioperative or late-onset complications after surgery between those taking or not taking antithrombotics. However, transurethral coagulation for hemostasis was needed in up to 14% of the antithrombotic therapy group. In another case series of 329 patients undergoing transurethral resection of the prostate, there were no differences in between those taking and not taking clopidogrel in intraoperative blood loss, transfusion, or secondary hemorrhage and clot retention after discharge.

Authors of a systematic review of 6 cohort studies found that antiplatelet monotherapy was associated with a modestly increased risk of post-sphincterotomy bleeding (OR 1.53, 95% CI 1.03-2.28) with a number needed to harm of 185 (95% CI 80-2272).

In a case series of 217 patients undergoing tracheostomy of whom 69 (31.8%) were on antithrombotic therapy during surgery and 148 (68.2%) were not, there were no significant differences in perioperative or postoperative bleeding; however, patients on anticoagulant therapy were 2.67 times more likely to experience 30-day mortality than those not on antithrombotic therapy although only one death was due to hemorrhage.

In a case series of 100 patients undergoing laparoscopic radical nephrectomy or nephroureterectomy, there were no differences in intraoperative blood loss, perioperative transfusion, readmission rate, or high-grade complications between the 36 patients taking antithrombotic agents and the 64 patients not on antithrombotic agents despite the former group more severe comorbidities.
Continuing VKAs during minor dental procedures does not confer an increase in clinically relevant major bleeding, but may cause a significant increase of nonmajor bleeding.

For dental procedures, ACCP 2022 guidelines recommend no discontinuation of VKA therapy and use of a pro-hemostatic agent such as tranexamic acid mouthwash 2 to 3 times daily pre- and post-procedure, if needed.

Authors of a retrospective chart review study of 179 patients on oral antithrombotic drugs undergoing dental surgery found that perioperative bleeding was associated with an 8-fold increase in postoperative hemorrhage and recommended close follow-up in these patients. Combination anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapy also increased postoperative bleeding risk. Complications did not require hospitalization.

Clinically significant major, nonmajor, or minor bleeding is significantly reduced in patients who receive a hemostatic agent (eg, epinephrine, topical hemostatic collagen) prior to or during the dental procedure.
ACCP 2022 guidelines suggest continuing ASA or P2Y12 inhibitor during the perioperative period.
In patients without a history of PCI with stent placement, clopidogrel can be stopped 5 to 10 days prior to the dental procedure.

In patients with a history of PCI with stent placement, clopidogrel should not be stopped prior to 6 weeks after PCI if a bare metal stent was placed, or prior to 12 months after PCI if a drug-eluting stent was placed.

Continue during the perioperative period. Similar to minor dental procedures, ACCP 2022 guidelines recommend continuation of VKA therapy for minor dermatologic or ophthalmologic procedures (very low-certainty evidence). VKA interruption may be preferred with procedures at higher bleeding risk such as complex retinal surgery.
ACCP 2022 suggests continuing aspirin or P2Y12 inhibitor during the perioperative period.
In patients without a history of PCI with stent placement, clopidogrel should be stopped 5 to 10 days prior to the dermatological procedure.

In patients with a history of PCI with stent placement, clopidogrel should not be stopped prior to 6 weeks after PCI if a bare metal stent was placed, or prior to 12 months if a drug-eluting stent was placed.

The American Society of Interventional Pain Physicians (ASIPP) 2019 guidelines note that interventional techniques can be categorized into low-risk, moderate-risk, and high-risk for decision-making around management of anticoagulant and antithrombotic therapy. Further, risk should be upgraded based on patient risk factors for bleeding and thrombosis. They encourage shared decision with patients to consider appropriate risks associated with continuation or discontinuation of antithrombotic or anticoagulant therapy.

Based on a systematic review of 57 manuscripts, including 10 guidelines, ASIPP concluded that high risk procedures are: cervical, thoracic, and high lumbar (above L4-L5) interlaminar epidural; cervical, thoracic and lumbar above L3 transforaminal epidural injections; spinal cord stimulator trial and implant; percutaneous adhesiolysis with interlaminar or transforaminal approach; percutaneous disc decompression (above L4/5); sympathetic blocks (stellate ganglion; thoracic splanchnic, celiac plexus); thoracic and cervical intradiscal procedures; vertebral augmentation, lumbar (above L4), thoracic and cervical; intrathecal catheter and pump implant; and interspinous prosthesis and minimally-invasive lumbar decompression.

Low-risk procedures include trigger point and muscular injections (including piriformis injection), peripheral joints and nerve blocks, sacroiliac joint and ligament injections and nerve blocks, caudal epidural injections, and ganglion impar blocks. Additional information on procedure categorization is available in the cited guideline.
There is fair evidence of excessive bleeding such as epidural hematoma formation during interventional techniques when antithrombotic therapy is continued.
ASIPP concluded that there is good evidence for discontinuation of anticoagulant therapy with warfarin.
Warfarin should be discontinued for high risk procedures, in the manner described above, and for low risk procedures based on risk factors. B
LMWH can be discontinued 24 hours prior to performing interventional techniques. B

ASIPP 2019 guidelines suggest discontinuation of anticoagulant therapy with heparin, dabigatran, argatroban, bivalirudin, lepirudin, desirudin, hirudin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, Betrixaban, and fondaparinux prior to interventional techniques with individual consideration of pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the drugs and individual risk factors to increase safety.

Pradaxa should be discontinued for 24 hours for paravertebral interventional techniques, for 2 to 4 days for epidural interventions in patients with normal renal function, and for longer periods of time in patients with renal impairment. C
Rivaroxaban should be discontinued for 24 hours prior to performing interventional techniques. C
ASIPP notes that if thromboembolic risk is high, antithrombotic therapy may be resumed 12 hours after the interventional procedure is performed.

The ASIPP 2019 guidelines concluded that there is good evidence supporting discontinuation of low dose ASA for high-risk and moderate-risk procedures for at least 3 days. A Low-dose ASA may be continued for low-risk or some intermediate-risk procedures based on moderate evidence. B

ASIPP found limited evidence that discontinuation of other antiplatelet therapy (clopidogrel, ticlopidine, Ticagrelor and prasugrel) avoids complications of significant bleeding and epidural hematomas. There is very limited evidence supporting the continuation or discontinuation of most NSAIDs, excluding aspirin, for 1 to 2 days and some for 4 to 10 days and decisions should be individualized. C
Patients who require an urgent surgical or other invasive procedure and require reversal of the anticoagulant effect should receive low-dose (2.5-5.0 mg) IV or oral vitamin K.
If more immediate reversal of the anticoagulant effect is desired, patients should receive fresh frozen plasma or another prothrombin concentrate in addition to low-dose IV or oral vitamin K.

There is no pharmacologic agent that can reverse the antithrombotic effect of aspirin or clopidogrel, which irreversibly inhibit platelet function. Consequently, patients who require an urgent surgical or other invasive procedure may be given transfused platelets, which would not be affected by prior administration of antiplatelet therapy.
For women requiring long-term VKA therapy who are attempting pregnancy, perform frequent pregnancy tests and substitute UFH or LMWH for warfarin when pregnancy is achieved.

For women attempting pregnancy who are taking a NOAC, the ACCP consensus statement is to switch to vitamin K antagonists rather than to LMWH while attempting pregnancy. At this time, NOACs should not be used during pregnancy or lactation.

The ACCP consensus opinion for women with AF receiving oral anticoagulants for stroke/thromboembolic prevention who become pregnant is to discontinue a VKA between weeks 6 and 12 and replace with LMWH twice daily (with dose adjustment according to weight and target anti- Xa level 4-6 h post-dose 0.8-1.2 U/mL). Use adjusted-dose LMWH (same target anti-Xa level) in the 36th week of gestation.

For women with acute VTE, use adjusted-dose LMWH throughout pregnancy or IV UFH for at least 5 days, followed by adjusted-dose UFH or LMWH for the remainder of the pregnancy and at least 6 weeks postpartum (Grade 1C+).
For women with a single episode of VTE associated with a transient risk factor that is no longer present, use antepartum clinical surveillance and postpartum anticoagulants (Grade 1C).

For women with a single episode of VTE and thrombophilia or strong family history of thrombosis and not receiving long-term anticoagulants, use antepartum prophylactic or intermediate dose LMWH or minidose or moderate-dose UFH, plus postpartum anticoagulants (Grade 2C).

For women with multiple (2+) episodes of VTE an/or women receiving long-term anticoagulants, use antepartum adjusted-dose UFH or adjusted-dose LMWH followed by long-term anticoagulants postpartum (Grade 2C).

For women with antiphospholipid antibodies (APLAs) and a history of multiple (2+) early pregnancy loses, preeclampsia, intrauterine growth retardations, or abruption, use antepartum aspirin plus minidose or moderate-dose UFH or prophylactic LMWH (Grade 2B).
For women with APLAs without prior VTE or pregnancy loss, use surveillance, minidose heparin, prophylactic LMWH, and/or low-dose aspirin (75-325 mg per day) (Grade 2C).

For pregnant women with prosthetic heart valves, use adjusted-dose LMWH twice a day throughout pregnancy, aggressive adjusted-dose UFH throughout pregnancy, or UFH or LMWH until the 13th week and then change to warfarin until the middle of the third trimester before restarting UFH or LMWH (Grade 1C).
For high-risk pregnant women with prosthetic heart valves, add low-dose aspirin (75-162 mg per day) (Grade 2C).

For women using dose-adjusted LMWH, ACCP recommend that LMWH be discontinued 22 to 24 hours before a cesarean section or regional anesthesia. When labor induction is performed, ACCP recommend discontinuing LMWH 24 hours before expected delivery or initiation of an epidural. Individual judgments can be based on advanced cervical maturity that may qualify a patient for discontinuation 12 to 24 hours before induction.

ACOG recommend that long-term antithrombotic therapy be interrupted and bridging therapy with LMWH be used until post-surgical antithrombotic treatment is therapeutic for women with a history of VTE or atrial fibrillation who are at high risk of thromboembolism. The same protocol should be used for women with mechanical heart values who are at high or moderate risk of thromboembolism.

For women with prior VTE at moderate risk of thromboembolism with high risk of bleeding or for women at low risk of thromboembolism, interrupt antithrombotic therapy and do not use bridging therapy; antithrombotic therapy should be resumed after surgery and mechanical prophylaxis with intermittent compression should be used during surgery and until long-term antithrombotic therapy is therapeutic. Other cases must be individualized and additional information is available in the ACOG bulletin.

list.listitem: The American College of Cardiology and the American Heart Association guidelines state that dual antiplatelet therapy should be given for at least 6 weeks after PCI and bare metal stent placement, and for at least 12 months after PCI and drug-eluting stent placement.

In a meta-analysis of quasi-experimental studies of patients on anticoagulation therapy for another reason (usually atrial fibrillation), authors concluded that triple therapy (aspirin + clopidogrel + oral anticoagulant) was associated with fewer cardiovascular events (OR 0.60; 95% CI, 0.42-0.86) and lower all-cause mortality (OR 0.59; 95% CI, 0.39-0.90) but higher risk of bleeding (OR 2.1; 95% CI, 1.05-4.29) after coronary artery stent placement. Based on these results, patients on anticoagulation therapy who are at low risk of bleeding might be considered for triple therapy following stent placement.

Among 2725 patients with atrial fibrillation who were within 5 days of undergoing PCI, dual therapy with either low or higher-dose dabigatran plus clopidogrel caused fewer major bleeding events than triple therapy with warfarin, aspirin, and clopidogrel and was noninferior for thromboembolic prevention.

However, in a cohort study of 7811 patients undergoing non-cardiac surgeries within 2 years of PCI in Veterans Affairs hospital, major adverse cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events were more frequent among those on triple therapy vs. duel therapy (11.3% vs. 4.9%, respectively).

To identify the optimal antithrombotic therapy during the peri-operative period for carotid endarterectomy, investigators used the Dutch Audit for Carotid Interventions registry including 12 317 patients of whom 31.0% of patients were treated with ASA, 32.4% with clopidogrel, 11.1% with ASA plus clopidogrel, 10.4% with ASA plus dipyridamole, 10.3% with VKA, and 4.8% with DOACs. There were no differences in the primary outcome of post-operative cervical bleeding needing re-intervention or intracranial hemorrhage during the first 30 days following the procedure between single-agent and dual-agent therapy. The authors concluded that, based on current guidelines, dual-antiplatelet therapy should be started immediately after stroke until 30 days after carotid endarterectomy followed by single-agent therapy, to possibly reduce risk of recurrence.

Authors of a Cochrane review concluded that for patients with symptomatic PAD treated by endovascular revascularization of the pelvic or femoropopliteal arteries, aspirin (50-300 mg) started prior to treatment appeared most safe and effective; continued aspirin (330 mg) combined with dipyridamole versus placebo reduced recurrent obstruction at 12 months follow-up. Peri-interventional treatment with LMWH in femoropopliteal obstructions resulted in significantly lower restenosis/reocclusion rates than with UFH.

In another Cochrane review, patients with symptomatic PAD undergoing infrainguinal bypass surgery with an artificial graft obtained slight benefit from aspirin on peripheral bypass graft patency but did not appear to benefit for cardiovascular outcomes or survival.
For patients undergoing infra-inguinal venous grafting, treatment with VKAs was more effective than aspirin in graft patency, limb salvage, and survival.

For increasing short-term patency of AV fistulae and grafts, Cochrane authors found low quality evidence that ticlopidine (an anti-platelet drug) had a beneficial effect but data were insufficient for comparing other treatments (eg, aspirin, clopidogrel, fish oil) against placebo to maintain patency.

When resuming antithrombotic therapy after a surgical or invasive procedure, it takes 2 to 3 days for a partial anticoagulant effect to begin after the start of warfarin and 3 to 5 hours for a peak anticoagulant effect to be reached after the start of low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH). Full warfarin anticoagulant effect takes 4-8 days.
ACCP 2022 recommends rapid resumption (12-24 hours) of the usual dose of warfarin post-procedure/surgery (very low-certainty evidence).
For aspirin, it takes minutes for an antiplatelet effect to begin and 3 to 7 days for peak inhibition of platelet aggregation to be reached after a maintenance dose of clopidogrel.
DOACs can be resumed 24 or more hours after low-moderate-bleed-risk procedures, and 48-72 hours after high-bleed-risk procedures.

In a case series of 366 patients with AF who underwent major non-cardiac surgery, antithrombotics (interrupted due to surgery) were resumed until discharge in only half (51.8%). Not reinstituting aspirin was associated with higher one-year mortality (17.6% vs. 34.8%).
